content.title: About
content.content: The opossum is a small marsupial native to North and South America. It is known for its ability to “play dead” when threatened. Opossums have a fur‑covered body, a long tail, and sharp teeth that allow them to eat both plant and animal matter.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Opossums are the only marsupials that live in North America.
They have a continuous tooth replacement system: baby teeth fall out and permanent teeth keep growing.
Opossums possess a natural resistance to the venom of cobras and some other poisonous snakes.
Unlike most mammals, opossums have a third eyelid that protects their eyes while feeding.
They can perform “thanatosis” – feigning death – to deter predators.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Opossum meat provides a high amount of complete protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low fat content
items.content: Compared with many other game meats, opossum meat is relatively low in fat, making it a lean dietary option.

items.title: Rich in iron
items.content: The meat is a good source of heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: It contains B12, B6, and niacin, supporting nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Opossum meat supplies zinc and phosphorus, important for immune health and bone strength.

items.title: Parasite risk
items.content: As with other wild game, opossums can carry parasites and diseases, so the meat must be thoroughly cooked.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Some individuals may develop an allergy to marsupial meat.

items.title: Organ toxicity
items.content: Liver and kidneys can accumulate toxins; it is advisable to avoid these organs.

items.title: Stress hormone content
items.content: Wild animals may have elevated cortisol levels, which can affect flavor and potential effects.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Opossum meat is commonly grilled, stewed, or pan‑seared as steaks. It should be marinated before cooking to mellow the flavor. In some cuisines it is used in sausages and pâtés.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh meat in the refrigerator at 0 °C–4 °C for no more than 2 days. For longer storage, freeze it in an airtight bag at –18 °C; it keeps well for up to 6 months. Thaw frozen meat in the fridge before cooking.
